facts.subject: Wheat-wearers
facts.statement: Wheat-wearer thralls are outside the Burg's law like cattle; a thrall's crimes, even murder, go unpunished unless her master punishes her.

refs.q: such folk are no more within the law than kine be

facts.subject: Wheat-wearers
facts.statement: Captive women are sold at the market-cross to the highest bidder; fair young ones fetch a good price.

refs.q: such of them as be fair, and that is the more part of the younger ones, fetch no ill penny

facts.subject: Wheat-wearers
facts.statement: All Wheat-wearer males taken are slain, by ancient oath; Dry Tree carles taken are also slain.

refs.q: thus we swore to do by all the greatest oaths that we might swear

facts.subject: Wheat-wearers
facts.statement: Wheat-wearer thrall women are good weavers of figured silk.

refs.q: Yet are the queens good websters

facts.subject: Burg of the Four Friths
facts.statement: Wheat-wearers stormed the lightly fenced town and held it for three generations; the Burg-folk rose at Yule and slew them.

refs.q: held them enthralled for three generations of men

facts.subject: Burg of the Four Friths
facts.statement: Afterwards the Burg was fortified, and the Forest Lord, captain, wedded the Fair Lady, granddaughter of the old lord.

refs.q: did we make the Burg strong and hard to win, as ye see it to-day

facts.subject: Burg of the Four Friths
facts.statement: By the War-smith's order all freemen learn war; women, thralls and aliens do other crafts and trade.

refs.q: let the women and thralls and aliens see to other craftsmanship and to chaffer

facts.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree
facts.statement: The burgher says the Dry Tree is no peril, its hunting keeps the Burg's men in trim, and they are "the chief deer" of the wood.

refs.q: they are the chief deer wherewith our wood is stocked

facts.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree
facts.statement: Sorcery and the wiles of their Queen make them hard to crush.

refs.q: because sorcery goes with them, and the wiles of one who is their Queen

facts.subject: Wheat-wearers
facts.statement: The burgher says conquering them outright would mean endless fighting, so the Burg raids instead.

refs.q: the battle would be to begin at every sun's uprising

facts.subject: Burg of the Four Friths
facts.statement: Strangers who neither serve nor trade are viewed with suspicion.

refs.q: here is the stranger looked upon with doubt, if he neither will take the wages of the Burg for battle, nor hath aught to sell

ledger.summary: At the Flower de Luce Ralph sees the big man in a sallet and white gaberdine (the man of the leafless tree) with a small cloaked bright-eyed companion leave the hall. Over supper townsmen explain the thralls: Wheat-wearer women taken in war, sold at the market-cross while all Wheat-wearer males are slain, and outside the Burg's law. An old burgher tells the Burg's history: conquest by the Wheat-wearers, three generations of thraldom, a Yule uprising, the Forest Lord and the Fair Lady, and the War-smith who made every freeman a warrior. He says the Dry Tree is kept alive as sport and protected by sorcery, and warns Ralph against asking questions. Roger swears to follow Ralph.
ledger.geography_notes: No new places; adds the Wheat-wearers as a neighbouring nation with towns, castles and land, beaten in battle by the Burg.
